1836 · Historical scholarship

Map of the Indian tribes of North America, about 1600 A.D. along the Atlantic, & about 1800 A.D. westwardly

Albert Gallatin; American Antiquarian Society

Gallatin assembled this map for an American Antiquarian Society publication in 1836. Its title distinguishes eastern depictions around 1600 from western depictions around 1800. Compare its historical naming and classifications with later maps; its labels do not define current communities or borders.

1929 reproduction; earlier map indexed 1724 · Indigenous knowledge / mediated copy

Catawba deerskin map: archival reproduction

Unidentified Indigenous maker; colonial copy associated with Francis Nicholson

An archival reproduction preserves a copied network of communities and paths drawn from Indigenous knowledge. The conventional Catawba title does not establish the maker’s identity. Colonial annotations and multiple copying stages make its production history essential context for interpretation.

[1755?] · Indigenous knowledge / mediated copy

Monongahela battlefield sketch

John Montrésor associated; unidentified Indigenous direction credited

This battlefield sketch credits Indigenous direction, while the catalog associates it with John Montrésor. That wording exposes a history of mediation and copying. It offers a focused example of Indigenous geographic knowledge entering a colonial military record, with its maker unnamed.

London, 1777 · Colonial cartography

Canada and neighboring borderlands, 1777

Claude Joseph Sauthier; William Faden

A British colonial map of southern Quebec and neighboring borderlands, compiled from French surveys. Its military and commercial framing offers evidence about colonial priorities and representations of Indigenous people. Read it as a historical viewpoint, without treating it as present territorial authority.

1639 design; surviving-copy dating differs · Colonial cartography

Manhattan and neighboring settlements

Joan Vinckeboons

This Dutch colonial map records settlements and landholding around Manhattan; Indigenous villages also appear in the archive’s guide. It invites comparison of ways of naming and representing inhabited places. The catalog and guide give differing dates for the surviving copy.

1891 · Federal survey / administration

Linguistic Stocks of American Indians North of Mexico.

John Wesley Powell

Powell grouped North American Indigenous languages into the linguistic stocks used by nineteenth-century federal ethnology. Read this as a historical classification project, including its names and large colored areas, alongside language and community accounts. These areas do not establish present boundaries.

1889 · Federal survey / administration

Indian territory: compiled under the direction of the Hon. John H. Oberly, Commissioner of Indian Affairs, by C.A. Maxwell

Charles A. Maxwell; United States Office of Indian Affairs

This Office of Indian Affairs map presents Indian Territory through federal administrative categories in 1889, with information about occupied lands, transfers and cessions. Its vocabulary belongs to that dated record. Examine federal mapping practices alongside the histories of the nations shown.

1900 · Federal survey / administration

Map of Choctaw Nation, Indian territory: compiled from official records of the United States Geological Survey

R. L. McAlpine; United States Department of the Interior

McAlpine compiled this federal map from United States Geological Survey records. The catalog identifies approved coal leases and claims, while the LOC guide places it among Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes reports. Read its land-administration context without treating it as a present-day jurisdiction map.

1851 · Historical map · metadata lead

[Map of the upper Great Plains and Rocky Mountains region]

Pierre-Jean De Smet (1801–1873), as named in the catalogue

Catalogued as an 1851 manuscript showing territories of named Indigenous peoples across the upper Plains and Rockies. De Smet's classifications belong to this historical document. Use for comparison with community accounts, not present boundaries; image labels and detail remain uninspected.

1814 · Historical map · metadata lead

A map of Lewis and Clark's track across the western portion of North America, from the Mississippi to the Pacific Ocean : by order of the executive of the United States in 1804, 5 & 6

Samuel Lewis; William Clark; Longman (Firm); Neele & Son, as named in the catalogue

Published in London in 1814, this expedition map offers a historical route across the western interior toward the Pacific. It is a record of United States exploration and its cartographers' framing. Specific Idaho-area Indigenous labels and image quality require visual verification.

[1890?] · Historical map · metadata lead

[Map of North America showing Indian tribes]

Producer not identified

An anonymously produced manuscript adds Indigenous labels to a printed North American base map. The archive dates it only approximately. Its continental scope may support Great Lakes comparisons, but attribution, individual labels and coloured areas need direct image review before detailed interpretation.

[1850] · Historical map · metadata lead

Map of a Reconnoissance between Fort Leavenworth on the Missouri River, and the Great Salt Lake in the Territory Of Utah, made in 1849 and 1850

Howard Stansbury, cartographer; John W. Gunnison, Charles Preuss and James W. Abert, contributors; United States Army Corps of Engineers; Ackerman Lithr, publisher

An Army reconnaissance map connects Fort Leavenworth with Great Salt Lake, showing tribal areas alongside routes, rivers and topography according to the catalogue. Read its geography within the expedition's perspective and period. Detailed Indigenous labels and boundaries remain visually unverified here.

A growing map room

This first selection brings archive records together. Some have a reusable preview; others open at the holding institution. The collection will grow, with more maps linked to relevant nations and regions as the evidence is reviewed.

Follow the originals

Original titles can contain outdated language. Archive descriptions and our inspection notes explain what was checked. A linked record is not a completed nation-level research review.
